newsitem.title: USA: Wisconsin bans insurance for $30 mln GO bond sale.
newsitem.headline: Wisconsin bans insurance for $30 mln GO bond sale.

text.p: Municipal bond underwriters were scratching their heads Monday over an unusual provision for an upcoming Wisconsin $30 million general obligation bond issue that bans the use of bond insurance.

The official notice of sale for the competitive issue stated that the successful bidder for the bonds must certify that neither the firm nor any other member of its underwriting syndicate obtained insurance for the deal.
The provision, however, does not prohibit insuring the bonds in the secondary market or with portfolio insurance.
"It's strange," said one underwriter. "I don't recall seeing something like that."
That reaction was echoed by underwriters at other major municipal bond firms.

Frank Hoadley, Wisconsin's capital finance director, said the provision was added to the Oct. 16 sale to stop a recent trend by underwriters who have been getting insurance for the state's competitive deals.
"There is absolutely no benefit to the state for having bond insurance," Hoadley said.

Hoadley said the acquisition of bond insurance adds to the spread for the deal. He added that while the insurance may make it easier for firms to sell the bonds, it doesn't affect the price of the bonds.

"Unenhanced deals do just as well," he said, pointing to other deals the state has sold with the state's GO ratings of double-A from Standard & Poor's Corp. and Moody's Investors Service and AA-plus from Fitch Investors Service.
Hoadley said that underwriters have obtained insurance for two state transportation revenue bond issues and one veterans housing GO bond issue over the past year.

With the upcoming issue, Hoadley said he expects a higher yield given the fact the housing GO bonds have special redemption provisions and are subject to alternative minimum tax. However, he pointed out that bond insurance would be irrelevent.
"None of those factors have anything to do with credit," he said.

He said the addition of bond insurance also adds to the state's work in coordinating documents and other materials for disclosure purposes. He added that given the proliferation of bond insurance there was a glut of insured paper in the market.
The insurance ban provision isn't expected to stop underwriters from bidding on the deal, according to Hoadley.
"This is a market that is starved for bonds," he said.
He added that the state was unable to find language for the insurance ban provision anywhere else and had to come up with it on its own.
Indeed underwriters said they had not seen such a provision before. One underwriter suggested that Hoadley was sending a message to the street that the state's ratings are good enough to stand alone.
"He's making a mountain out of a mole hill," the underwriter said.
One insurer expressed surprise that an issuer would take such an action that could potentially raise its borrowing costs.
--Karen Pierog, 312-408-8647
